title: Fast Cashiers in the Next Lane
text:
Economists Alexandre Mas and Enrico Moretti, at the University of California, Berkeley, wanted to know whether working next to a productive colleague makes people work harder. They found an ideal setting in a national supermarket chain, which recorded every item every cashier scanned.

In the stores they studied, cashiers worked in shifts that were scheduled in ways that had nothing to do with who was fast or slow. That meant that at random moments, a cashier might find a particularly fast colleague arriving at a nearby register, or leaving. The researchers could then see how everyone else's speed changed.

When a highly productive cashier joined the shift, the others sped up. The effect was not small: an increase in the average productivity of coworkers was followed by a measurable increase in each cashier's own pace.

The arrangement of the registers revealed why. The speedup appeared only when the fast cashier was positioned where they could see the slower one working. Being observed by a fast colleague mattered, while seeing a fast colleague did not. The authors linked this to social pressure among coworkers who saw each other regularly.
lesson: Effort is contagious when people can see each other's work. Place your strongest performers where teammates notice them, and let good norms spread.
location: Stores of a national supermarket chain, USA
source: Mas, A., and Moretti, E. (2009). Peers at work. American Economic Review, 99(1), 112-145.
